aperture.text: The hole in the lens, and how wide it is open. Written as an f-number: f/2.8 is wide, f/8 is narrow. It decides how much light gets in and how deep the sharp band is.

bokeh.text: What the out-of-focus parts of a picture look like, as opposed to how much of the picture is out of focus. A Japanese word, borrowed into photography in the 1990s.

crop-factor.text: How many times smaller a sensor is than a 36 by 24 mm frame, corner to corner. The P950's is 5.6, so its 357 mm lens frames like a 2000 mm lens on a big camera.

depth-of-field.text: The band of distances that looks sharp in a photograph. It widens as the aperture narrows, as the subject gets farther away, and as the lens gets shorter.

diffraction.text: The softening every lens suffers when the hole is small, because light spreads as it passes an edge. On a small sensor it is already visible by f/4, which is why narrowing down past that trades one kind of sharpness for another.

exposure.text: How much light the picture was made from, set by the aperture and the shutter together. A picture can be over-exposed (too bright, whites lost) or under-exposed (too dark, shadows lost).

exposure-compensation.text: A dial that tells the camera to make the picture brighter or darker than its meter thinks right. The first thing to reach for with snow, sand or a bird against a bright sky.

focal-length.text: How strongly a lens bends light, in millimetres; in practice, how narrow a wedge of the world it takes in. Quoted on compact cameras as the equivalent on a 36 by 24 mm frame.

golden-hour.text: The hour after sunrise and before sunset, when the sun is low, the light is warm and shadows are long. Nature photography is largely the art of being out in it.

histogram.text: A chart of how many pixels in a picture are at each brightness. The only honest way to judge exposure on a screen in daylight.

hyperfocal.text: The nearest distance you can focus on and still have the horizon look sharp. Focusing there wrings the most depth of field out of a landscape.

iso.text: How much the camera amplifies what the sensor caught. Raising it brightens a picture taken in too little light, and brings up the grain with it. The name comes from the film-speed standard.

noise.text: The roughness left when too few photons were counted, seen as grain in flat areas and false colour in shadows. More a property of the light than of the camera.

panning.text: Swinging the camera with a moving animal while the shutter is open, so it comes out sharp against a streaked background.

raw.text: The sensor's own numbers, saved before the camera turns them into a picture. It keeps more of the highlights and lets white balance and exposure be reconsidered afterwards.

shutter-speed.text: How long the sensor collects light, in fractions of a second. It decides how movement is recorded, in the scene and in your hands.

stop.text: A doubling or halving of the light. One stop on any of the three dials, so a stop given up on one can be taken back on another.

stabiliser.text: Lens elements that shift to cancel small movements of the camera, bought in stops of slower shutter. It works on your hands and does nothing about a moving subject.

white-balance.text: What the camera is told the colour of the light was, so that white things come out white. Set in kelvin: warm light is a low number.
